szoveg_eredeti:
Educational Climate and Self-Efficacy Predict Higher AI Literacy in Nursing Students

A cross-sectional investigation of 333 undergraduate nursing students from two Chinese medical colleges has identified three distinct latent profiles of artificial intelligence literacy, revealing that while a majority exhibit moderate competency, higher literacy is strongly tied to supportive institutional environments and personal confidence. Published in Frontiers in Medicine, the study evaluated how personal characteristics and institutional settings relate to students’ technological preparedness.

The investigative team, based at Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital and Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, framed the inquiry around the expanding role of computational technologies in clinical environments. Rapid advances and deployments of artificial intelligence applications have transformed nursing discipline standards and routine patient-care procedures, establishing artificial intelligence literacy as an essential competency for contemporary healthcare practitioners. National education policies and professional guidelines have accordingly emphasized an urgent requirement for systematic artificial intelligence instruction in undergraduate curricula, prompting the researchers to identify underlying competency patterns to inform evidence-based educational strategies.

The cross-sectional investigation utilized a structured data gathering protocol that combined a self-designed general demographic questionnaire with three established psychometric instruments.

The investigators conducted latent profile analysis using Mplus version 8.3 to evaluate class solutions and determine the optimal number of competency profiles among the participating nursing undergraduates.

The latent profile analysis resolved the student population into three distinct competency categories characterized by low, moderate, and high artificial intelligence literacy. The largest proportion of the sample fell into the moderate literacy subgroup, which encompassed 58.0 percent of participants, representing 193 individual students.

Subsequent multivariate modeling using R3STEP multinomial logistic regression demonstrated that educational climate, self-efficacy, and academic stage were significantly associated with profile membership. A more favorable educational climate, higher general self-efficacy scores, and freshman academic standing, evaluated relative to senior status, served as statistically significant predictors of placement in the high literacy profile, with all associations achieving statistical significance at the P < 0.05 threshold. Similarly, a more favorable educational climate and freshman status relative to senior standing emerged as significant associated factors predicting membership in the moderate literacy profile at the P < 0.05 level.

Based on these observed associations, the researchers concluded that nursing colleges should implement stratified, targeted instructional programs tailored to specific baseline proficiency tiers. The investigators further recommended optimizing the broader institutional atmosphere and expanding dedicated support mechanisms for students from rural backgrounds and those in lower literacy groups to facilitate the broader intelligent transformation of nursing education.

Subject of Research: Artificial intelligence literacy profiles and associated factors among undergraduate nursing students

Article Title: Latent profiles of artificial intelligence literacy and associated factors among undergraduate nursing students: a cross-sectional study

Article References: Zhang, Q., Yu, Q., Wang, G., Zeng, Z., Rao, X., Liu, S., & Wang, Y. (2026). Latent profiles of artificial intelligence literacy and associated factors among undergraduate nursing students: a cross-sectional study. Frontiers in Medicine, 13, Article 1935146. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1935146

Keywords: artificial intelligence literacy, undergraduate nursing students, latent profile analysis, educational climate, general self-efficacy, nursing education, cross-sectional survey, Chinese medical colleges, multinomial logistic regression, Mplus, SPSS, freshman nursing students, senior nursing students, clinical practice competencies, educational environment, rural student support, Tianjin Medical University, Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine
